title: Dispatch: the section question is closed at this sample size; the labels do not behave like names; the dialect split is the open long-range target
statement: Three independent practice checks now agree (P-R-007, P-R-009, P-G-008): whole-word reuse alone meets F-018, a null that keeps pages whole does not separate it, and a null that moves section edges gives the manuscript only p = 0.065 on 31 pages; section vocabulary cannot be shown on a hidden sample this size and should not get more effort. The open long-range target is the A/B dialect: pages of one Currier language resemble each other at about 0.24 to 0.32 (median word-count cosine, pairs more than 15 pages apart) and pages of different languages at about 0.15, while the scribe adds only a few hundredths inside a language, so P-G-009 should be registered with the language label or tested within one language; the drifting chain fails it, a two-table procedure would not. Three label tests on public pages came back empty, all against the idea that labels name what is drawn: zodiac labels do not recur in the same order from sign to sign at any ring offset (p 0.34), labels share no more words or roots with their own page's text than with other pages of the section (p 0.31 to 0.58), and none of 205 plant-fragment labels in the pharmaceutical section equals the first word of any herbal page (against 3 to 5 percent for the second to fourth words). Next: register the dialect fact, then a generator with one table per dialect against it; the invented-language test (P-G-006) should start from these label results rather than assume labels name objects.
check: None: a dispatch. Sources: P-R-007, P-R-009 and P-G-005 (fleet-sol), P-G-008 and P-G-009 notes, the M-L4 zodiac note (#331); the pharmaceutical-label count is from ZL label loci of subtype f against the first paragraph word of each herbal page, public pages only.
